subject: English
description: Grammar + idiom + structure errors, plus trickier subject-verb cases

questions.stem: Spot the error: 'She has been living here (A) / since three years (B) / and is very happy (C) / with her neighbours. (D)'
questions.explanation: 'Since' + a point in time (since 2020). For a duration, use 'FOR'. Correct: 'for three years' (not 'since three years').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Spot the error: 'The furniture in my office (A) / are new (B) / and very (C) / comfortable. (D)'
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is an UNCOUNTABLE noun — takes singular verb. 'The furniture IS new' (not 'are'). Similar: luggage, information, advice, news.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Spot the error: 'One of the boys (A) / are absent (B) / today due to (C) / illness. (D)'
questions.explanation: 'One of + plural noun' takes SINGULAR verb. 'One of the boys IS absent today' (not 'are'). Similarly: 'Each of the boys is...' / 'Neither of the boys is...'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Spot the error: 'He is senior (A) / than me (B) / by ten years (C) / of experience. (D)'
questions.explanation: Latin-origin adjectives ending in -ior take 'TO', not 'THAN'. Correct: 'senior TO me'. Similar: junior, superior, inferior, prior, posterior — all take 'to'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Spot the error: 'The chairman along with (A) / his team members (B) / were invited (C) / to the meeting. (D)'
questions.explanation: 'A along with B' takes a verb agreeing with A (the principal subject). Chairman is singular → 'WAS invited'. 'Together with / as well as / accompanied by' follow the same rule — they do NOT make the subject plural.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Spot the error: 'If I would have (A) / known about it, (B) / I would have (C) / helped you. (D)'
questions.explanation: 3rd conditional: 'If + past perfect, would have + V3'. 'If I HAD known... I would have helped...'. Never 'if + would have' in the IF-clause.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Spot the error: 'The committee (A) / have decided (B) / to release the (C) / funds next week. (D)'
questions.explanation: 'Committee' is a COLLECTIVE NOUN. When the group is treated as a single unit (and verb in Indian English usually takes singular), use 'HAS'. 'The committee has decided...' (British English sometimes allows plural when emphasising individual members, but the exam-standard form is singular.)
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Spot the error in: 'He is an European (A) / who has worked as (B) / an engineer in (C) / this firm for years. (D)'

options.option_text: The sentence contains no grammatical error

questions.explanation: Part A is wrong: 'European' begins with the consonant sound /juː/, so the article must be 'a', not 'an'. The rule is governed by pronunciation, not spelling — compare 'an MBA' (vowel sound) vs 'a university' (consonant sound). Option B is a common trap since 'has worked' (present perfect for ongoing employment) is grammatically valid.

questions.stem: Spot the error in: 'The doctor suggested (A) / that the patient rests (B) / for at least (C) / a week. (D)'

options.option_text: 'for at least' should be 'at least for'
The sentence contains no grammatical error

questions.explanation: Part B is wrong: verbs of recommendation — 'suggest', 'recommend', 'insist', 'demand' — trigger the mandative subjunctive, requiring the bare infinitive in the that-clause regardless of the subject. 'Rests' (third-person -s form) must be 'rest'. Option A is tempting but 'suggested' in the simple past is perfectly correct here.

questions.stem: Spot the error in: 'Despite of his poor health (A) / he attended (B) / all the scheduled (C) / lectures regularly. (D)'

options.option_text: 'Despite of' is wrong; correct form is 'Despite'
'all the' should be 'all of the' correctly
The sentence contains no grammatical error

questions.explanation: Part A is wrong: 'despite' is itself a preposition equivalent to 'in spite of', so adding 'of' after it is redundant and incorrect. Correct forms are 'Despite his poor health' or 'In spite of his poor health'. Option C is a deliberate trap — both 'all the lectures' and 'all of the lectures' are standard English, so Part C carries no error.

questions.stem: Spot the error in: 'Either the director (A) / or his assistants (B) / is responsible (C) / for the oversight. (D)'

options.option_text: The sentence contains no grammatical error

questions.explanation: Part C is wrong: the proximity rule applies with 'either...or' — the verb agrees with the subject immediately before it. 'Assistants' is plural, so the verb must be 'are responsible', not 'is responsible'. Option B is the classic trap: 'either...or' is a standard affirmative correlative and there is no rule requiring it to become 'neither...nor'.

questions.stem: Spot the error in: 'No sooner had (A) / the bell rung (B) / then the children (C) / rushed out. (D)'

options.option_text: 'rung' should be 'rang' since the action is past
The sentence contains no grammatical error

questions.explanation: Part C is wrong: the fixed correlative is 'no sooner...than', never 'no sooner...then'. 'Then' indicates a time sequence; 'than' is grammatically required by the idiom. Option B is the strongest trap: after auxiliary 'had', the past participle 'rung' is correct — substituting simple past 'rang' would actually introduce an error, not fix one.

questions.stem: Spot the error in: 'Seldom I have witnessed (A) / such dedication (B) / among the young (C) / officers. (D)'

options.option_text: 'Seldom I have' needs inversion: 'Seldom have I'
'among the young' should be 'between the young'
The sentence contains no grammatical error

questions.explanation: Part A is wrong: negative or restrictive adverbials fronted for emphasis — 'seldom', 'rarely', 'hardly', 'never', 'little', 'not only' — trigger obligatory subject-auxiliary inversion. 'Seldom I have witnessed' must be 'Seldom have I witnessed'. Option C traps students who confuse 'among' (three or more) with 'between' (exactly two); referring to a group of officers, 'among' is the correct preposition.

questions.stem: Spot the error in: 'The principal, as well as (A) / his teachers, have been (B) / summoned to appear (C) / before the board. (D)'

options.option_text: 'as well as' should be changed to 'and'
The sentence contains no grammatical error

questions.explanation: Part B is wrong: 'as well as', 'along with', 'together with', and 'in addition to' are parenthetical connectors, not coordinating conjunctions. The grammatical subject remains 'The principal' (singular), so the verb must be 'has been', not 'have been'. Option A is the strongest trap — replacing 'as well as' with 'and' would create a compound plural subject and make 'have been' correct, but the original connector is itself grammatically acceptable.
